explanationCorrect: Self-hosted runners are selected by labels; listing multiple labels like [self-hosted, gpu] requires a runner that carries all of them, targeting your GPU machine.
explanationIncorrect: A single arbitrary string like gpu-runner-only only matches if a runner literally has that exact label, and it omits the self-hosted label that distinguishes your fleet from GitHub-hosted runners. uses: is for referencing actions, not selecting runners. There is no runner: label key; runner selection is expressed solely through runs-on labels.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Which mechanism lets an organization publish a starter workflow that repositories can adopt from the Actions tab?

options.text: A workflow-templates directory in the organization's .github repository
A required-workflows setting on each repo
A branch named starter in every repository
Enabling GitHub Pages for the organization

explanationCorrect: Placing workflow YAML plus a JSON properties file in the workflow-templates directory of the org's special .github repository surfaces those templates as starter workflows for member repositories.
explanationIncorrect: Required workflows enforce running a workflow but are a different feature from offering an adoptable starter template. A branch named starter has no special meaning to Actions and would not appear as a template. GitHub Pages publishes static websites and is entirely unrelated to distributing starter workflows.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: For security, why is it recommended not to run self-hosted runners on public repositories?

options.text: Forked pull requests could run untrusted code on your infrastructure
Public repositories cannot use self-hosted runners at all
Self-hosted runners cannot access the internet
GitHub bills extra minutes for public self-hosted runs

explanationCorrect: A malicious fork can open a pull request whose workflow executes arbitrary code; on a self-hosted runner that code runs on your own machine and network, which is why GitHub warns against it for public repos.
explanationIncorrect: It is technically possible to attach self-hosted runners to public repositories; the guidance is about risk, not an outright block. Self-hosted runners typically do have internet access, so that is not the concern. GitHub does not bill minutes for self-hosted runners at all since you provide the hardware, so extra billing is not the reason.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization admin wants secrets that many repositories share, managed centrally. What is the right feature?

options.text: Organization-level secrets with a repository access policy
Copying the same repository secret into each repo by hand
Committing the secret to a shared config file
Storing the secret as an environment variable in each workflow

explanationCorrect: Organization secrets are defined once and made available to selected or all repositories through an access policy, giving central management without duplication.
explanationIncorrect: Hand-copying a repository secret into every repo is exactly the duplication and drift that org secrets eliminate. Committing a secret to a file exposes it in the repository history and is a serious security mistake. Putting the value in a plain env variable in each workflow neither centralises it nor keeps it secret, since env values are visible in the workflow definition.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Which report helps an enterprise understand how many Actions minutes and storage are being consumed?

options.text: The billing and usage metrics for Actions in the organization or enterprise settings
The repository's Insights traffic graph
The Dependency graph
The Security overview

explanationCorrect: Actions minute and storage consumption is reported under the billing and usage sections of organization or enterprise settings, where you can also download usage reports.
explanationIncorrect: The Insights traffic graph tracks views and clones of a repository, not Actions consumption. The Dependency graph lists software dependencies for security and does not measure compute usage. The Security overview aggregates code and secret scanning alerts, which is unrelated to minutes and storage billing.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: You want to restrict the default permissions of GITHUB_TOKEN across all repositories in an organization to read-only by default. Where is this best set?

options.text: In the organization Actions settings, choosing the read-only default workflow permissions
By editing every workflow to add permissions: read-all
By rotating the token manually each day
By disabling the GITHUB_TOKEN feature

explanationCorrect: Organization Actions settings include a default workflow permissions choice; setting it to read-only applies that baseline to repositories, and workflows can still request more with an explicit permissions block.
explanationIncorrect: Editing every workflow is error-prone and does not enforce a baseline for new or unmodified workflows the way the org setting does. GITHUB_TOKEN is minted per run and does not need manual daily rotation, so that does not address default permissions. Disabling the token would break most workflows that need any repository access, which is far broader than tightening the default.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: What is the purpose of a runner group?

options.text: To control which organizations or repositories may use a set of self-hosted runners
To automatically scale GitHub-hosted runners
To group workflow jobs so they share a runner
To assign labels to GitHub-hosted runners

explanationCorrect: Runner groups are an access-control boundary for self-hosted runners, letting admins decide which repositories or organizations are allowed to send jobs to the runners in that group.
explanationIncorrect: Runner groups do not scale GitHub-hosted runners; those scale automatically and are not organised into your groups. They do not cause jobs to share a runner; each job still gets its own runner assignment. Labels apply to runners for targeting, but a runner group is about access scope, not label assignment on GitHub-hosted machines.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Which approach keeps sensitive cloud credentials out of long-lived secrets when workflows deploy to a cloud provider?

options.text: OpenID Connect (OIDC) federation to obtain short-lived credentials at run time
Storing the access keys as organization secrets
Printing the credentials to the log for auditing
Hard-coding the keys in the workflow file

explanationCorrect: OIDC lets a workflow exchange a signed identity token for short-lived cloud credentials via a trust policy, removing the need to store static long-lived keys as secrets.
explanationIncorrect: Storing static access keys as org secrets still keeps long-lived credentials around, which is exactly the risk OIDC removes. Printing credentials to logs exposes them even though the runner masks known secrets, and it is never an auditing practice. Hard-coding keys in the workflow file commits them to the repository, the worst option for secret handling.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An enterprise wants certain reusable workflows to run on every repository regardless of what the repo's own workflows contain. Which feature fits?

options.text: Required workflows configured at the organization level
A branch protection rule requiring status checks
A CODEOWNERS file listing the security team
A repository ruleset limiting who can push

explanationCorrect: Required (organization) workflows let admins enforce that a specified reusable workflow runs on pull requests across selected repositories, independent of the repositories' own workflow files.
explanationIncorrect: Branch protection status checks can require a check to pass but do not themselves inject or run a centrally defined workflow across many repositories. CODEOWNERS routes review requests and does not run any workflow. A ruleset limiting who can push governs write access, not the automatic execution of an enforced workflow.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: Why might an organization mirror popular third-party actions into an internal repository and reference those copies?

options.text: To pin a reviewed version and reduce supply-chain risk from upstream changes
Because external actions cannot be used without mirroring
To make workflows run faster by avoiding the network
Because GitHub deletes third-party actions after 90 days

explanationCorrect: Mirroring lets a team vet a specific version of an action, control when it updates, and insulate their workflows from unexpected or malicious upstream changes, tightening the software supply chain.
explanationIncorrect: External actions can be used directly, so mirroring is a security choice rather than a requirement. Performance is not the motivation; the runner still checks out the action, and any speed difference is negligible compared with the supply-chain benefit. GitHub does not delete third-party actions after 90 days, so that is not a reason to mirror.

stem: How does one workflow call a reusable workflow defined in another file?

options.text: With a job that sets uses: owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref
With a step that sets uses: for the workflow file
By copying the reusable workflow's jobs into the caller
With needs: pointing at the other workflow

explanationCorrect: A reusable workflow is invoked at the job level with uses: pointing to the workflow file and a ref, for example owner/repo/.github/workflows/build.yml@v1.
explanationIncorrect: Steps cannot call a whole workflow with uses:; that job-versus-step distinction matters because reusable workflows are referenced by a job, not a step. Copying jobs into the caller defeats reuse and is not how the feature works. needs only orders jobs within a single workflow and cannot invoke a separate reusable workflow.

stem: What must a reusable workflow declare so that callers can invoke it?

options.text: on: workflow_call
on: workflow_dispatch
reusable: true at the workflow root
A callable: block under jobs

explanationCorrect: A workflow becomes reusable by triggering on workflow_call, which also lets it declare inputs, secrets, and outputs for its callers.
explanationIncorrect: workflow_dispatch enables a manual Run button, not invocation by another workflow. There is no reusable: true root key; reusability is expressed through the workflow_call trigger. There is no callable: block under jobs; the contract for callers is defined by the workflow_call event, not by a job-level key.

stem: A caller needs to pass a secret to a reusable workflow. Which caller syntax forwards all of the caller's secrets?

options.text: secrets: inherit
secrets: all
with: secrets: '*'
env: SECRETS: inherit

explanationCorrect: secrets: inherit on the calling job passes all of the caller's secrets to the reusable workflow without naming each one individually.
explanationIncorrect: secrets: all is not valid syntax; the keyword is inherit. Secrets are not passed through with:, which is for inputs, and there is no '*' wildcard there. env: with a SECRETS key does not forward secrets to a reusable workflow; secret forwarding is handled by the dedicated secrets key on the calling job.

stem: How does a caller read an output produced by a reusable workflow?

options.text: Via needs.<job>.outputs.<name> after listing the reusable job in needs
Via steps.<job>.outputs.<name>
The caller cannot access reusable workflow outputs
Via env.<name> automatically

explanationCorrect: A reusable workflow declares outputs under workflow_call, and the caller reads them through needs.<jobId>.outputs.<name>, which requires depending on that job.
explanationIncorrect: steps.<job> is wrong because a reusable workflow is invoked as a job, not a step, so its results live in the job outputs, not the steps context. Callers absolutely can read reusable workflow outputs when they are declared, so claiming otherwise is false. Outputs are not injected into env automatically; you must reference them through the needs context.

stem: What is the difference between using a marketplace action and calling a reusable workflow?

options.text: An action is a single unit invoked by a step; a reusable workflow packages one or more entire jobs invoked at the job level
They are the same feature with different names
A reusable workflow can only run on self-hosted runners
An action cannot take inputs but a reusable workflow can

explanationCorrect: Actions are the smallest reusable unit, run as a step inside a job, while reusable workflows bundle complete jobs and are called at the job level, so they operate at different granularities.
explanationIncorrect: They are not the same feature; the step-versus-job distinction is exactly what separates them. Reusable workflows run on whatever runners their jobs specify, not only self-hosted ones. Actions certainly can take inputs through with:, so the claim that they cannot is false.

stem: For supply-chain security, what is the strongest way to pin a third-party action you consume?

options.text: Reference it by full commit SHA rather than a tag or branch
Reference it by the moving major tag such as @v3
Reference it by @main
Reference it without any ref so it always updates

explanationCorrect: A full commit SHA is immutable, so pinning to it guarantees you run exactly the reviewed code even if a tag is later moved to point at malicious commits.
explanationIncorrect: A major tag like @v3 is convenient but can be re-pointed by the author, so it is weaker than a SHA. @main tracks the tip of the default branch and can change at any time, offering the least stability. Omitting a ref is not even valid for most actions and certainly would not provide a pinned, reviewed version, so it is the least secure.

stem: You call a reusable workflow and want to pass a build target as an input. Which caller key carries inputs?

options.text: with:
inputs:
env:
params:

explanationCorrect: The calling job passes declared inputs to a reusable workflow through the with: map, matching the input names the workflow_call trigger defines.
explanationIncorrect: The reusable workflow declares its parameters under inputs:, but the caller supplies values with with:, so using inputs: on the caller is wrong. env: sets environment variables and does not map to a reusable workflow's declared inputs. There is no params: key for passing inputs; the caller-side key is with:.

stem: A workflow uses actions/checkout before running an action that operates on the repository. Why is the checkout step usually required first?

options.text: The runner starts with an empty workspace, so the repository must be checked out before the code is available
Checkout is only needed for private repositories
Checkout installs the action's dependencies
Checkout authenticates the GITHUB_TOKEN

explanationCorrect: A fresh runner has no repository content in its workspace; actions/checkout clones the repository so subsequent steps and local actions can read the source.
explanationIncorrect: Checkout is needed for public repositories too whenever a step must read the code, so it is not private-only. It does not install an action's dependencies; JavaScript actions ship their own bundled dependencies. It does not authenticate GITHUB_TOKEN; the token is provided to the job independently and checkout merely uses it to fetch the code.

stem: There is a limit to how deeply reusable workflows can be nested when calling one another. What is that maximum nesting depth of reusable workflow calls?

options.text: Up to four levels of nested reusable workflow calls
Unlimited nesting is allowed
Only one level; a reusable workflow cannot call another
Up to ten levels

explanationCorrect: GitHub allows a chain of nested reusable workflow calls up to four levels deep, so a caller can reach reusable workflows that themselves call others within that limit.
explanationIncorrect: Nesting is not unlimited; there is a documented cap, so relying on infinite depth would eventually fail. It is more than one level, so the claim that a reusable workflow cannot call another is incorrect. Ten is simply the wrong number; the supported depth is four.

stem: How can you consume a specific released version of a reusable workflow so it does not change unexpectedly?

options.text: Reference the workflow file with a version tag or SHA after the @, such as @v2 or a commit SHA
Reference it without a ref and rely on the latest
Copy the workflow into your repo each release
Use needs: to lock the version

explanationCorrect: The @ref part of the reusable workflow reference selects the version; a tag like @v2 or a commit SHA pins it so upstream changes on other refs do not affect you.
explanationIncorrect: A reference without a ref is not valid for reusable workflows; you must specify a branch, tag, or SHA. Copying the workflow each release abandons reuse and reintroduces maintenance you were trying to avoid. needs only orders jobs and has nothing to do with selecting a version of a reusable workflow.

stem: A team wants to share a cache of build dependencies between separate workflow runs. Which action is designed for that?

options.text: actions/cache, keyed on a hash of the lockfile
actions/upload-artifact, which persists across runs indefinitely
actions/checkout with a cache flag
A self-hosted runner is the only way to cache

explanationCorrect: actions/cache stores and restores directories keyed by a value such as a lockfile hash, so dependencies fetched in one run can be reused by later runs.
explanationIncorrect: upload-artifact is for passing files between jobs of the same run or for download after a run; artifacts have retention limits and are not a dependency cache. actions/checkout has no caching flag that shares dependency directories across runs. Self-hosted runners might retain state, but caching is available on hosted runners too through actions/cache, so it is not the only way.

stem: Where do you find, evaluate, and copy usage snippets for community actions?

options.text: The GitHub Marketplace
The repository Wiki tab
The Projects board
The Discussions tab

explanationCorrect: The GitHub Marketplace lists published actions with descriptions, versions, and ready-to-copy usage snippets, and it is where you discover and vet community actions.
explanationIncorrect: The Wiki holds free-form documentation for a single repository and is not a catalogue of actions. Projects boards track work items and issues, not action discovery. Discussions is a forum for questions and conversation, not the curated listing with usage snippets that Marketplace provides.

stem: A reusable workflow declares a required secret named DEPLOY_KEY under workflow_call. What happens if the caller does not provide it and does not use inherit?

options.text: The run fails because a required secret was not supplied
The secret defaults to an empty string silently
GitHub prompts the user interactively for the value
The caller's repository secrets are used automatically

explanationCorrect: When a reusable workflow marks a secret as required under workflow_call, the caller must pass it explicitly or via inherit; omitting it causes the run to fail validation.
explanationIncorrect: A required secret does not silently default to empty; that is the point of marking it required. Actions runs are non-interactive, so GitHub never prompts a user for a value during a run. Caller secrets are not passed automatically unless you use secrets: inherit or name them explicitly, so they would not be supplied on their own.

stem: You want only one deployment workflow to run at a time for a given environment, cancelling any in-progress run when a newer one starts. Which configuration achieves this?

options.text: A concurrency group with cancel-in-progress set to true
A matrix strategy with max-parallel set to 1
The timeout-minutes key on the deploy job
A needs dependency on the previous run

explanationCorrect: The concurrency key groups runs by a key you choose and, with cancel-in-progress: true, cancels any already-running run in that group when a new one is queued.
explanationIncorrect: max-parallel only limits how many matrix jobs within a single run execute at once, not how many separate runs overlap. timeout-minutes caps how long a job may run before it is killed, unrelated to overlapping runs. needs establishes ordering between jobs in the same run and cannot reference a separate workflow run at all.

stem: A step needs to expose a computed value so later steps in the same job can read it as a step output. Where should the step write it?

options.text: Append name=value to the file referenced by $GITHUB_OUTPUT
Use the deprecated ::set-output workflow command
Export it with the shell export keyword
Append it to the file referenced by $GITHUB_ENV

explanationCorrect: Writing name=value to the file at $GITHUB_OUTPUT registers a step output that later steps read via steps.<id>.outputs.<name>.
explanationIncorrect: The ::set-output command still nominally works but is deprecated and disabled on many runners, so it is not the current mechanism. A plain shell export only affects the current step's process and is gone in the next step. Writing to $GITHUB_ENV sets an environment variable for later steps, which is a different mechanism from a named step output and is read differently.

stem: A job has continue-on-error: true on a flaky step. A later step uses if: steps.flaky.outcome == 'failure'. What is the difference between the outcome and conclusion of that step?

options.text: outcome is the raw result before continue-on-error is applied; conclusion is the result after it is applied
outcome and conclusion are always identical for a step
conclusion is the raw result; outcome is adjusted by continue-on-error
outcome only exists for jobs, not steps

explanationCorrect: A step's outcome is its result before continue-on-error is honored, while conclusion reflects the result after continue-on-error may have turned a failure into success.
explanationIncorrect: The two differ precisely when continue-on-error is in play, so calling them always identical is wrong. The roles are reversed in the option that claims conclusion is the raw value. Both outcome and conclusion exist on steps as well as jobs, so restricting outcome to jobs is incorrect.

stem: You want a workflow to run only when files under the docs/ directory change on pushes to main. Which trigger configuration is correct?

options.text: on.push with branches: [main] and paths: ['docs/**']
on.push with branches: [main] and paths-ignore: ['docs/**']
on.pull_request with paths: ['docs/**']
on.push with tags: ['docs/**']

explanationCorrect: Combining branches: [main] with paths: ['docs/**'] makes the push trigger fire only when the push targets main and touches at least one file under docs/.
explanationIncorrect: paths-ignore does the opposite, skipping the run when only docs/ files change. Using pull_request responds to PR events rather than pushes to main, which is a different trigger. The tags filter matches Git tag names, not file paths, so a glob like docs/** there would match tag references, not changed files.

stem: A cleanup step must run whether earlier steps succeeded or failed, but not if the job was cancelled. Which if expression fits?

options.text: if: ${{ !cancelled() }}
if: ${{ always() }}
if: ${{ success() }}
if: ${{ failure() }}

explanationCorrect: !cancelled() evaluates true on both success and failure but false when the run is cancelled, which is exactly the requested behavior.
explanationIncorrect: always() runs the step even on cancellation, so it does not exclude the cancelled case. success() runs only when all prior steps passed, skipping the failure case. failure() runs only when a prior step failed, skipping the success case, so neither status function alone covers both success and failure while excluding cancellation.

stem: Your matrix build should keep running the other combinations even if one fails, and you also want to test three combinations at most simultaneously. Which two strategy keys do you set?

options.text: fail-fast: false and max-parallel: 3
fail-fast: true and max-parallel: 3
continue-on-error: true and concurrency: 3
fail-fast: false and matrix.parallel: 3

explanationCorrect: fail-fast: false stops one failing combination from cancelling the rest, and max-parallel: 3 caps how many matrix jobs run concurrently.
explanationIncorrect: fail-fast: true is the default that cancels remaining jobs on the first failure, the opposite of what is wanted. continue-on-error changes how a job's failure is reported rather than the matrix cancellation behavior, and concurrency is not a numeric matrix throttle. matrix.parallel is not a real key; the correct throttle lives under strategy as max-parallel.

stem: Two jobs must share a compiled binary: job build produces it and job deploy consumes it. Jobs run on separate runners. What is the standard way to pass the file between them?

options.text: Upload it with actions/upload-artifact in build and retrieve it with actions/download-artifact in deploy
Write it to $GITHUB_ENV in build so deploy reads it
Store it in the actions/cache and rely on cache restore
Reference the file directly since jobs share a filesystem

explanationCorrect: Artifacts are the intended mechanism to move build outputs between jobs: upload in the producer job and download in the consumer job.
explanationIncorrect: $GITHUB_ENV only passes environment variable strings within a single job, not files across jobs. actions/cache is meant for speeding up repeated dependency restores keyed by a hash, not for reliably handing a specific build output to a downstream job. Jobs run on isolated runners and do not share a filesystem, so referencing the path directly fails in deploy.

stem: A workflow_dispatch trigger defines an input named environment of type choice with options staging and production. How does a step read the chosen value?

options.text: ${{ inputs.environment }} or ${{ github.event.inputs.environment }}
${{ env.environment }} only
${{ secrets.environment }}
${{ vars.environment }}

explanationCorrect: Manual dispatch inputs are available through the inputs context and, for backward compatibility, through github.event.inputs.
explanationIncorrect: The env context holds environment variables you defined, not dispatch inputs. The secrets context exposes configured secrets, and vars exposes configuration variables; neither is where a workflow_dispatch input value lands, so reading the input through them returns nothing.

stem: By default a workflow's GITHUB_TOKEN gets read/write permissions at the repository level. To follow least privilege you want a job that only reads code and writes check results. Which permissions block is appropriate?

options.text: permissions: { contents: read, checks: write }
permissions: write-all
permissions: {} with contents left implicit
permissions: read-all

explanationCorrect: Declaring only contents: read and checks: write grants exactly the scopes the job needs and drops all others to none, matching least privilege.
explanationIncorrect: write-all restores broad write access, the opposite of narrowing scopes. An empty permissions map sets every scope to none, so the job could not write check results. read-all grants read on all scopes but no write, so the job could not create check results either.

stem: You want to call a reusable workflow stored in another repository at a fixed release. Which uses reference is valid?

options.text: uses: octo-org/shared/.github/workflows/build.yml@v2
uses: octo-org/shared/build.yml@v2
uses: ./.github/workflows/build.yml from another repo
run: octo-org/shared/build.yml@v2

explanationCorrect: A cross-repository reusable workflow is referenced as owner/repo/.github/workflows/file.yml@ref, including the full path under .github/workflows and a ref.
explanationIncorrect: Dropping the .github/workflows/ path segment makes the reference invalid because reusable workflows must live in that directory. The ./ relative form only works for a workflow in the same repository, not another one. run is for shell commands, not for calling a reusable workflow, which must use the uses keyword at the job level.

stem: A caller wants a called reusable workflow to have access to all of the caller's secrets without listing each one. What does the caller specify?

options.text: secrets: inherit
secrets: all
with: secrets
permissions: inherit

explanationCorrect: secrets: inherit passes every secret available to the caller down to the reusable workflow without naming them individually.
explanationIncorrect: secrets: all is not valid syntax; the keyword is inherit. with is for passing inputs, not secrets, so listing secrets under it does nothing. permissions controls GITHUB_TOKEN scopes and has no inherit form that forwards secrets, so it cannot accomplish secret passing.

stem: A reusable workflow declares outputs under workflow_call.outputs, mapping them from a job's outputs. How does the calling job reference one of those outputs?

options.text: needs.<callJobId>.outputs.<outputName>
steps.<callJobId>.outputs.<outputName>
jobs.<callJobId>.outputs.<outputName>
env.<outputName>

explanationCorrect: The reusable workflow's declared outputs surface on the calling job as outputs, so a dependent job reads them via needs.<callJobId>.outputs.<name>.
explanationIncorrect: The steps context refers to steps within the current job, not to another job's outputs. There is no jobs context usable inside a workflow to read another job's outputs at runtime that way. env holds environment variables, not the outputs a called workflow exposes, so none of these reach the reusable workflow's outputs.

stem: You want to pin a third-party marketplace action to an immutable reference so a moved tag cannot change what code runs. Which reference is safest?

options.text: A full-length commit SHA, e.g. actions/checkout@8f4b7f8...
A major version tag, e.g. actions/checkout@v4
A branch name, e.g. actions/checkout@main
No ref, letting it default to the latest release

explanationCorrect: A full commit SHA is immutable, so pinning to it guarantees the exact code runs even if tags or branches are later moved.
explanationIncorrect: A major version tag like v4 is a moving reference the maintainer can repoint to new commits. A branch such as main advances with every merge, giving no reproducibility. Omitting the ref is not even valid for actions and would not pin anything, so only the SHA is truly immutable.

stem: A composite action you consume needs two inputs, region and stage. How do you pass them when calling it in a step?

options.text: Provide a with: block containing region and stage
Provide an env: block containing region and stage
Pass them as positional args after uses
Provide a secrets: block containing region and stage

explanationCorrect: Action inputs are supplied via the with map on the step that references the action.
explanationIncorrect: env sets environment variables for the step rather than binding declared action inputs. Actions do not accept positional arguments after uses; inputs are named. secrets is not how inputs are passed to an action step, so only the with block maps to the action's declared inputs.

stem: There is a limit on how deeply reusable workflows may call other reusable workflows. What is that nesting limit including the top-level caller?

options.text: Up to four levels of reusable workflows
Unlimited nesting
Exactly two levels
Up to ten levels

explanationCorrect: GitHub allows a chain of up to four levels of reusable workflows, counting the initial caller and up to three nested calls.
explanationIncorrect: Nesting is not unlimited; a fixed cap exists to prevent runaway chains. A limit of exactly two would forbid common patterns that GitHub actually supports. Ten is higher than the documented maximum, so a chain that deep would be rejected before running.

stem: You reference a Docker container action from a public registry in a step. Which uses syntax is correct?

options.text: uses: docker://alpine:3.19
uses: image://alpine:3.19
run: docker run alpine:3.19
container: alpine:3.19 under uses

explanationCorrect: A step can run a published container directly with uses: docker://<image>:<tag> using the docker:// scheme.
explanationIncorrect: There is no image:// scheme for the uses keyword. Using run with docker run is a shell command, not a container action reference, and does not use the Actions container-action mechanism. container is a job-level key for a service or job container, not a value you place under uses in a step.

stem: A workflow calls a reusable workflow and needs to pass a numeric input build_number defined under workflow_call.inputs. How is it supplied?

options.text: Under the calling job's with: block, e.g. with: { build_number: 42 }
As an environment variable named build_number
Under a needs: block on the calling job
As a secret named build_number

explanationCorrect: Inputs declared under workflow_call are passed by the caller through the with map on the job that references the reusable workflow.
explanationIncorrect: An environment variable is not automatically bound to a declared workflow_call input. needs controls job ordering, not input passing. A secret is a separate channel from inputs and would not populate an input declared under workflow_call.inputs, so with is the only correct place.

stem: When a caller passes secrets: inherit to a reusable workflow in a different repository within the same organization, what is required for that to succeed?

options.text: The reusable workflow's repository must be granted access to be used by the caller's repository
Nothing extra; any repo can call any other repo's workflows
The caller must copy all secrets into the called repo first
The workflows must live in the same repository

explanationCorrect: Cross-repository reuse requires that the reusable workflow's repository allow access from the calling repository, configured through Actions access settings.
explanationIncorrect: Access is not automatic; without granting it the call is rejected. Copying secrets into the called repo would defeat the purpose of inherit and is unnecessary once access is granted. Requiring both to live in the same repository contradicts the premise of a cross-repository call, which GitHub supports once access is configured.

stem: You are writing a JavaScript action. Which file must exist at the action's root and declare runs.using along with the entry point?

options.text: action.yml (or action.yaml)
workflow.yml
package.json
Dockerfile

explanationCorrect: Every action is defined by an action.yml (or action.yaml) metadata file that declares inputs, outputs, and the runs configuration including using and main.
explanationIncorrect: workflow.yml is not an action metadata filename; workflows live under .github/workflows. package.json describes an npm package but is not the action metadata file Actions reads. A Dockerfile is only needed for a Docker container action and still must be referenced from action.yml, so the metadata file is always required.

stem: In a composite action, one shell step computes a value and a later shell step in the same action needs it as a step output. How does the first step publish it?

options.text: Echo name=value into $GITHUB_OUTPUT and give the step an id
Set it with the outputs key directly on the step
Return it from the step's run command
Write it to action.yml at runtime

explanationCorrect: Composite action steps publish outputs the same way workflow steps do: append name=value to $GITHUB_OUTPUT and reference it through the step id.
explanationIncorrect: There is no outputs key placed directly on an individual shell step to set values; step outputs go through the file. A run command's exit or stdout is not captured as a named output automatically. action.yml is static metadata and is not rewritten at runtime, so writing to it is not how outputs are produced.

stem: You want your action to expose an output named result that consumers read as steps.<id>.outputs.result. Where must result also be declared?

options.text: Under outputs in action.yml
Under inputs in action.yml
In the consuming workflow's env block
In a separate outputs.yml file

explanationCorrect: An action's outputs must be declared in the outputs section of action.yml so consumers can reference them predictably.
explanationIncorrect: inputs declares values passed into the action, not values it emits. The consuming workflow's env cannot declare an action's output contract; that belongs to the action. There is no separate outputs.yml convention; the metadata for outputs lives in action.yml itself.

stem: For a JavaScript action, why is it common practice to commit a bundled dist/index.js produced by a tool like ncc rather than the raw source with node_modules?

options.text: The runner does not run npm install for an action, so dependencies must be bundled into the committed entry file
Bundling encrypts the source to hide it
GitHub only executes TypeScript, so bundling transpiles it
Bundling is required to publish to the Marketplace and has no runtime effect

explanationCorrect: When an action runs, the runner executes the referenced entry file directly without installing dependencies, so the code and its dependencies must be bundled into a committed file.
explanationIncorrect: Bundling does not encrypt or hide source; the output is still readable JavaScript. The runner executes JavaScript, not TypeScript directly, but transpilation is a separate concern from why bundling is needed. Bundling has a real runtime effect precisely because no install step runs, so calling it purely a Marketplace formality is wrong.

stem: A Docker container action needs to run some logic after the job's other steps complete, similar to a cleanup hook. Which action.yml keys support pre and post logic for a JavaScript action?

options.text: runs.pre and runs.post pointing to scripts run before and after main
steps.before and steps.after
jobs.pre and jobs.post
hooks.setup and hooks.teardown

explanationCorrect: A JavaScript action can declare runs.pre and runs.post scripts that execute before and after the main entry point, useful for setup and cleanup.
explanationIncorrect: There are no steps.before or steps.after keys in action metadata. jobs.pre and jobs.post are not action metadata keys either; jobs belong to workflows. hooks.setup and hooks.teardown are invented names; the actual keys are pre and post under runs.

stem: You want to give consumers of your action a recognizable icon and color on the Marketplace listing. Where is that configured?

options.text: Under the branding key in action.yml
In the repository's README front matter
In a marketplace.json file
In the workflow that uses the action

explanationCorrect: The branding section of action.yml lets you set an icon and color used on the action's Marketplace listing.
explanationIncorrect: A README has no front matter that controls Marketplace branding. There is no marketplace.json convention for this. A consuming workflow cannot set the branding of an action it merely calls; branding is metadata owned by the action in action.yml.

stem: In a composite action, each run step must specify one setting that standalone workflow steps can inherit from defaults. What is it?

options.text: shell, which is required on every run step in a composite action
runs-on, chosen per step
container, required per step
environment, required per step

explanationCorrect: Composite action run steps must each declare a shell explicitly because they do not inherit a workflow-level default shell.
explanationIncorrect: runs-on selects the runner for a whole job, not a step inside an action, and is not set per composite step. container is a job-level setting, not a required per-step key in composite actions. environment is a deployment protection concept at the job level, not something each composite step declares, so shell is the required per-step key.

stem: You maintain a popular action and want consumers pinned to v3 to automatically receive non-breaking fixes. What release practice supports this?

options.text: Move a v3 major tag to point at each new v3.x release
Delete old releases so only v3 remains
Ask consumers to always reference the main branch
Publish only full SHAs and no tags

explanationCorrect: Maintaining a moving major tag such as v3 that you repoint to each compatible v3.x release is the conventional way consumers on @v3 receive non-breaking updates.
explanationIncorrect: Deleting old releases breaks anyone pinned to a specific version and does not create a moving major tag. Pointing consumers at main exposes them to unreleased and possibly breaking changes rather than curated fixes. Publishing only SHAs prevents the very major-tag convenience the scenario asks for, since consumers would have to change the SHA for every fix.

stem: An input in your action should be optional with a fallback value used when the caller omits it. How do you express that in action.yml?

options.text: Set required: false and provide a default under that input
Set required: true and provide a default
Add the input under outputs with a default
Provide the fallback only in the workflow, not the action

explanationCorrect: Marking an input required: false with a default lets callers omit it while the action still receives the fallback value.
explanationIncorrect: Marking it required: true forces callers to supply it, contradicting optional behavior. Inputs are declared under inputs, not outputs, so putting it there is wrong. Defining the fallback only in the workflow would not make the action itself supply a default when other callers omit the input, so the default belongs in action.yml.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An enterprise wants only specific actions to be usable across all organizations, blocking arbitrary Marketplace actions. Which control enforces this?

options.text: An allow list of permitted actions in the Actions policy settings
A branch protection rule on the default branch
A required status check named actions-allowed
A CODEOWNERS entry for .github/workflows

explanationCorrect: Actions policies let an enterprise or organization restrict which actions may run, including an allow list of specific actions and patterns.
explanationIncorrect: Branch protection governs merges into branches, not which actions workflows may reference. A status check gates merges based on a job result and does not restrict which actions exist. CODEOWNERS requests reviews for changed paths but cannot block an unlisted action from being invoked, so the allow list policy is the right control.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A team registers self-hosted runners and wants to ensure only workflows from a specific set of repositories can use a runner group. What do they configure?

options.text: Scope the runner group to selected repositories in its access settings
Add the repositories to the runner's labels
Set runs-on to the repository name
Give each repository the runner's registration token

explanationCorrect: Runner groups have access policies that restrict which repositories or organizations may send jobs to the runners in that group.
explanationIncorrect: Labels route jobs to runners by capability but do not enforce which repositories are allowed to use them. runs-on selects runners by label, not by naming a repository, and does not restrict access. Sharing a registration token would let a repo add its own runners, not scope access to an existing group, so the group access policy is correct.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: A security review flags that self-hosted runners on public repositories are risky. Why does GitHub recommend against self-hosted runners for public repos?

options.text: Forked pull requests could run untrusted code on your infrastructure
Public repos cannot use secrets at all
Self-hosted runners cannot check out public code
GitHub-hosted runners are mandatory for private repos only

explanationCorrect: On a public repository, a malicious fork's pull request could execute attacker-controlled code on your self-hosted runner, so GitHub advises against that combination.
explanationIncorrect: Public repos can use secrets, though they are restricted for fork PRs, so a blanket no-secrets claim is false. Self-hosted runners can absolutely check out public code. GitHub-hosted runners are not restricted to private repos; the real reason is the untrusted-code execution risk from forks.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization wants a default GITHUB_TOKEN that is read-only unless a workflow explicitly requests more. Which setting achieves this org-wide?

options.text: Set the default workflow token permissions to read-only in Actions settings
Delete the GITHUB_TOKEN secret
Add permissions: read to every workflow manually
Disable Actions entirely for the organization

explanationCorrect: The organization Actions settings include a default permissions choice for GITHUB_TOKEN, and setting it to read-only applies unless a workflow declares higher scopes.
explanationIncorrect: GITHUB_TOKEN is generated per run and cannot be deleted as a secret. Editing every workflow by hand is error prone and not an org-wide control, which is exactly what the default setting provides. Disabling Actions removes the feature altogether rather than making the token read-only, so the default-permissions setting is the correct lever.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: You need centralized visibility into who triggered workflow runs and changes to Actions settings across the enterprise. Where do you look?

options.text: The enterprise or organization audit log, which records Actions-related events
The individual run logs of each workflow only
The repository's Insights traffic graph
The Dependabot alerts page

explanationCorrect: The audit log captures Actions-related administrative and workflow events across the organization or enterprise, giving centralized visibility.
explanationIncorrect: Individual run logs show one run at a time and lack settings-change history, so they are not centralized. The traffic graph reports clones and views, not Actions governance events. Dependabot alerts concern vulnerable dependencies, unrelated to who changed Actions settings, so the audit log is the right source.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: To control monthly spending on GitHub-hosted runner minutes and storage for private repositories, what does an organization set?

options.text: A spending limit for Actions in the billing settings
A timeout-minutes value on every job
A concurrency group for all workflows
A retention period for artifacts only

explanationCorrect: Billing settings allow an Actions spending limit that caps overage charges for runner minutes and storage beyond the included amounts.
explanationIncorrect: timeout-minutes limits a single job's duration but does not cap total monthly spend across all runs. Concurrency limits overlapping runs, not cumulative billed usage. An artifact retention period reduces storage over time but is not the account-level spending cap, which is set in billing.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An enterprise wants runners that scale up automatically to meet demand and scale to zero when idle, using ephemeral runners. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Actions Runner Controller (ARC) on Kubernetes managing ephemeral runners
A single always-on self-hosted runner VM
Increasing the GitHub-hosted runner concurrency limit
Adding more labels to one static runner

explanationCorrect: Actions Runner Controller runs on Kubernetes and provisions ephemeral, autoscaling runners that expand under load and can scale to zero when idle.
explanationIncorrect: A single always-on VM neither autoscales nor scales to zero. Adjusting GitHub-hosted concurrency does not give you ephemeral self-hosted autoscaling on your own infrastructure. Adding labels to one static runner changes routing, not capacity or autoscaling, so ARC is the intended solution.

domain: Manage GitHub Actions in the enterprise
stem: An organization wants to reuse a set of standardized workflow templates that any repository can adopt from a central place. Where are these organization workflow templates stored?

options.text: In a workflow-templates directory of the organization's .github repository
In each repository's .github/workflows directory only
In a templates branch of every repository
In the organization's wiki

explanationCorrect: Organization-level starter workflows live in the workflow-templates folder of the special .github repository, from which any repo can create a workflow.
explanationIncorrect: Placing them only in each repo's workflows folder makes them local, not shared templates. There is no convention of a templates branch in every repository for this. The wiki holds documentation, not runnable starter workflows, so the .github repository's workflow-templates folder is the right location.
